title: Stone axes and adzes

identification.basis: The dictionary gives three words for axe, one of them glossed 'originally a stone axe'. Roth (1904) recorded the Bloomfield axe cement and a Bloomfield word for the stone, and Anderson (1996) describes the hafted axe, its materials and its cutting power from Kuku Yalanji accounts in the 1970s.

summary: The **[kulbanmuku](word:kulbanmuku)**, 'axe, originally a stone axe', was the tool that opened the trees: it felled the canoe logs, cut the steps up a honey tree, chopped out the [sugarbag](entry:native-bees) and the [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub), and took the bark sheets for [troughs](entry:bark-troughs) and huts [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]. The head was a ground-edged stone, a *celt* in Roth's word, and across Queensland the same head served as axe, adze or wedge depending on how it was held and hafted [ref:roth1904]. On the Bloomfield the head was tied into a handle of big lawyer cane with bark fibre or wallaby sinew and cemented with beeswax mixed with brown-cedar resin; Kuku Yalanji men told Anderson such an axe could fell softwoods up to a metre through and hardwoods to about 40 cm [ref:anderson1996]. Steel axes were the most valued trade goods of the early station days, and men worked for settlers to get them [ref:anderson1996]. How the stone head itself was shaped and ground is on the [stone](entry:stone) page; this page is the tool, its handle, its cement and its work.

infobox.label: Head
infobox.value: A ground-edged stone 'celt', often a water-worn pebble; diorite, basalt and similar hard rock

infobox.label: Handle
infobox.value: Bloomfield: a length of big lawyer cane bent round the head; elsewhere a bent wooden lath

infobox.label: Binding
infobox.value: Bark fibre or wallaby sinew, cemented with beeswax and brown-cedar resin (yikari)

infobox.label: Could cut
infobox.value: Softwoods to about 1 m through, hardwoods to about 40 cm

infobox.label: Jobs
infobox.value: Canoe logs, honey trees, grub logs, bark sheets, steps up trees; and as an adze, hollowing

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary has three words: **[kulbanmuku](word:kulbanmuku)** 'axe, originally a stone axe'; **[waymbil](word:waymbil)** 'axe'; and **[warrbi](word:warrbi)**, which is both 'axe' and a 'house made of grass, beehive house' [ref:hershberger1982]. For the head, Roth's list of local names for a stone celt gives, for the Bloomfield (KYE), *jangkawabi*, built on **[jangka](word:jangka)** 'stone' [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982]. For the cement, Roth recorded the Bloomfield gum *t-chaln-ji* 'used for fixing together the haft and shaft of spears, and in the old days (R. Hislop) was employed for fixing the stone-celt into its handle'; the dictionary's **[jalnji](word:jalnji)** is a poison-nut tree whose gum 'is not poisonous, used for making spears', and **[yikari](word:yikari)** is 'hardened beeswax, hardened with ironwood root juice', the spear and axe cement [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982]. The verbs: **[nyandal](word:nyandal)** 'to chop', **[nyurrbal](word:nyurrbal)** 'to grind, sharpen'; **[jalngkun](word:jalngkun)** 'sharp', **[dudu](word:dudu)** 'blunt'; and **[kadil](word:kadil)**, the 'sharp sound or crashing sound, as of an axe cutting wood, or a tree falling' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body:
**The head.** Roth, who had examined hundreds, argued that sorting stone celts into 'axes, adzes, wedges, scrapers' was mostly a European habit: 'the same celt may be used both as an axe or adze', the wedge-shaped celt of the Batavia and Pennefather rivers 'was used both as an axe, e.g., for cutting into trees, and as an adze, e.g., for hollowing out', the Bloomfield people 'undoubtedly used their axes as wedges', and Aboriginal evidence agreed that these were tools, not fighting weapons [ref:roth1904]. Most heads were made from water-worn pebbles chosen for being close to the shape already, so that only the edge had to be ground; others were broken from rock in place by fire or flaking. The Queensland rocks that made celts include diorite, basalt, argillite and serpentine [ref:roth1904]. Two local types stood out to him: a large, oval, slab-like, double-edged head with a groove round its middle, almost peculiar to the Herberton ranges, and a small, square, wedge-shaped celt peculiar to the Peninsula [ref:roth1904].

**The handle.** Across the far north and west the handle was a lath of wood bent double at its middle, the stone fixed in the bend with twine and beeswax or cement, and the two limbs bound together just below the stone and again at the grip. On Cape York the binding went only next to the stone, so the limbs crossed and gripped the head tighter, like a pair of pincers, when the diverging ends were squeezed [ref:roth1904]. There is no evidence that a Queensland celt was ever set in the fork of a stick, and some were used in the hand with no handle at all, as Cook saw on the Endeavour River [ref:roth1904].

**The Bloomfield axe.** Anderson's informants described it: 'The celts were tied onto a handle made of a portion of large lawyer cane and secured there by bark fibre or wallaby sinew and a gum mixture of beeswax mixed with resin from *Canarium australasicum*', the brown cedar [ref:anderson1996]. With hardwoods a downward chopping stroke was used rather than a horizontal one [ref:anderson1996]. The men carried their axes in belts of wallaby sinew or plaited hair [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Axe, adze, wedge or hammer?
sections.body:
- **Axe**: the edge in line with the handle, swung to cut across the grain [ref:roth1904].
- **Adze**: the same head turned so the edge is across the handle, pulled towards the body to hollow and shave; the canoe tool [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Wedge**: the head used alone, driven into a split; Roth says the Bloomfield people used their axes this way [ref:roth1904].
- **Hammer-stone**: unground, used for roughing out other stones and for pounding; see [stone](entry:stone) [ref:roth1904].
- **Grooved head**: a groove right round a wedge-shaped head means a handle, and probably use as both axe and adze by re-setting it [ref:roth1904].
- **A big butt**: a head whose back end is much bigger than its edge was probably used unhafted, because a handle would let it slip backwards under a heavy blow [ref:roth1904].
- **An old axe-head in an oven**: around the Annan and Endeavour rivers discarded heads were used as oven stones, which is why so few were left by 1900 [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Steps cut up a trunk**, one each side, to reach a bee hive; Anderson noted these 'on many trees in the Bloomfield area in the late 1970s' [ref:anderson1996].
- **Felled honey trees**: 'It is surprising to see how hard the Bloomfield blacks work in cutting down a big tree to get a hive', Le Souef wrote in 1894 [ref:anderson1996].
- **Bark scars** from troughs, canoes and hut sheets; see [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs) [ref:roth1904].
- **Grinding grooves** on sandstone near water where edges were ground; see [stone](entry:stone) [ref:roth1904].
- **A ground-edged stone on the surface** of a camp or an old oven is an artefact and is protected; leave it where it lies [ref:acha2003].
- **The sound**: *[kadil](word:kadil)*, the crack of an axe in wood or a tree coming down [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where the stone and the handle come from
sections.body:
Hard fine-grained stone for the head: diorite, basalt, argillite, serpentine [ref:roth1904]. At Karma Waters the ridges are Hodgkinson Formation greywacke, siltstone and slate, and the river's bed is full of water-worn pebbles of it, the raw material Roth says most heads began as [ref:jcu-carbine] [ref:kw-about] [ref:roth1904]. Good heads also travelled: Bulletin 14 records stone and other goods passing hand to hand along trade routes across the Peninsula [ref:roth1910].

For the handle, big [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) (**[mawar](word:mawar)**, 'the vine of the lawyer cane') in the rainforest country of the Bloomfield; a bent wooden lath in the open country [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982]. For the binding, bark fibre or wallaby tail [sinew](entry:sinew) (**[biyal](word:biyal)**) [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982]. For the cement, beeswax from the [native bees](entry:native-bees), brown-cedar resin, and the ironwood root juice that hardens *yikari*; see [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) and [ironwood](entry:ironwood) [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: What the axe did in the country
sections.body:
The axe sits at the start of most of the chains in this guide. It felled the candlenut, red cedar and cotton tree for [canoes](entry:canoes), whose insides were then burnt out and scraped with adzes [ref:anderson1996]. It opened the trees for [sugarbag](entry:native-bees): 'Hafted stone axes were used to obtain both the grubs and the bee hives', the nest hole enlarged with the axe, steps cut up the trunk, or the whole tree brought down [ref:anderson1996]. It split the rotten logs for [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub) [ref:anderson1996]. It cut the bark sheets for [troughs](entry:bark-troughs) and [huts](entry:huts-and-shelters) [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904]. It broke the bones of a crocodile before cooking [ref:anderson1996]. It also marks the woodland: a stand of old [bloodwoods](entry:bloodwood) with cut steps and bark scars is a place that was lived in, and the hollows the cockatoos nest in are often the hollows the honey came from [ref:anderson1996].

In the other direction, the axe depended on the country: on the right stone, on lawyer cane, on wallaby sinew, on beeswax from a healthy bee population and on brown-cedar resin, the trade in which Roth recorded [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904]. When steel came it displaced the stone head but not the handle-maker's and the honey-hunter's knowledge; men 'undertook any amount of work for a European settler in return for these tools' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The axe's busiest season was the dry, when sugarbag was hunted and the tree bases were checked and tapped for hollowness in the late dry; canoe and bark work came after the first storms when the sap had risen [ref:anderson1996]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- Felling trees for [canoes](entry:canoes); hollowing them as an adze [ref:anderson1996].
- Opening and felling [honey](entry:native-bees) trees; cutting steps to climb them [ref:anderson1996].
- Splitting rotten logs for [grubs](entry:witchetty-grub) [ref:anderson1996].
- Cutting bark for [troughs](entry:bark-troughs), [huts](entry:huts-and-shelters) and canoes [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].
- Splitting wood, as a wedge [ref:roth1904].
- Butchering large game: the Bloomfield crocodile 'bashed with an axe to break the bones' before it went on the fire [ref:anderson1996].
- Not fighting: Roth's Aboriginal informants were clear the celt was a tool [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Hafting a Bloomfield axe
sections.body:
The head's own making (choosing the pebble, roughing out, grinding the edge) is on the [stone](entry:stone) page. To make it a tool [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904]:

1. **Cut a length of big lawyer cane** long enough to bend double round the head with two limbs for a grip [ref:anderson1996].
2. **Bend it round the head** so the stone sits in the bend, edge outwards [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].
3. **Bind the two limbs together** close below the stone with bark-fibre twine or wallaby tail sinew; in the north-and-west style, bind again at the grip; in the Cape York style, bind only next to the stone so the crossed limbs grip the head like pincers when squeezed [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].
4. **Cement it.** Heat beeswax, mix it with brown-cedar resin (or use *yikari*, beeswax hardened with ironwood root juice), and work the warm cement round the head and over the binding; let it set hard [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
5. **Use it right.** Downward chopping strokes on hardwood, not horizontal ones; softwoods to about a metre through, hardwoods to about 40 cm [ref:anderson1996].
6. **To adze**, re-set the same head across the handle and pull the strokes towards you on charred timber [ref:roth1904].
7. **Keep the edge** by grinding on sandstone with water (*nyurrbal*) [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- A stone head in a cane haft can loosen; check the cement before a heavy stroke and keep the stroke downward and away from the legs [ref:anderson1996].
- Felling: a honey tree felled with an axe or a chainsaw comes down with the bees still in it; sugarbag bees do not sting, but hornets and paper wasps share hollows [ref:anderson1996].
- Stone artefacts, scarred trees and grinding grooves are protected under the *Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Act 2003*; do not collect, move or sell them [ref:acha2003].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: By 1904 Roth called the making of a celt 'a lost art in Queensland', and by the 1970s Bloomfield bush camps ran on steel axes, which were already the prized tools of the 1890s [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]. The knowledge that survives is the hafting, the cement and the work: where the honey trees are, which bark peels, how a log is hollowed. Old stone heads turn up on the station's creek banks and camps; they are cultural heritage, and under the duty of care in the *Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Act 2003* they stay where they are [ref:acha2003]. Native title holders' gathering rights under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* cover taking timber and bark for personal and communal use [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[kulbanmuku](word:kulbanmuku)* 'axe, originally a stone axe'; *[waymbil](word:waymbil)* 'axe'; *[warrbi](word:warrbi)* 'axe; house made of grass'; *[jangka](word:jangka)* 'stone'; *[jundi](word:jundi)* 'pumice stone, carborundum stone'; *[nyandal](word:nyandal)* 'to chop'; *[nyurrbal](word:nyurrbal)* 'to grind, sharpen'; *[jalngkun](word:jalngkun)* 'sharp'; *[dudu](word:dudu)* 'blunt'; *[kadil](word:kadil)* 'sharp sound, as of an axe cutting wood'; *[yikari](word:yikari)* 'hardened beeswax'; *[jalnji](word:jalnji)* the gum tree 'used for making spears'; *[mawar](word:mawar)* 'the vine of the lawyer cane'; *[biyal](word:biyal)* 'sinew' [ref:hershberger1982].
